715.title: The Song of Deborah (Judges 5:1–12)
715.hook: the war is sung again, and she calls herself "a mother in Israel"
715.howItsDone: The Song of Deborah is read in synagogue as the haftarah on the Shabbat when the Song at the Sea, Exodus 15, is read from the Torah, known as Shabbat Shirah, the Sabbath of song.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jael at her tent door, where the war ended. Your line was blessed in the tent. Today, the same story again, as a song.

For a while, nobody used the main roads. Travelers took the back paths. Village life stopped. That's how the song remembers the bad years, and it's a picture anyone who has lived through a frightening time might recognize: empty streets, people keeping out of sight, everyone going the long way round. Chapter four told the war as a story. Chapter five tells it again, and this time it's sung. It opens: "Then sang Deborah and Barak the son of Abinoam on that day."
screen: `NOBODY USED THE MAIN ROADS.` → `CHAPTER FOUR TOLD IT; CHAPTER FIVE SINGS IT.` → `THEN SANG DEBORAH AND BARAK.`

segments.voice: The song doesn't begin with the battle. It begins with the people who showed up: praise the Lord, when the people offered themselves willingly. It calls on kings and princes to listen: I will sing to the Lord. And before any fighting, it remembers the God of Sinai, when the earth trembled and the mountains flowed. Then it names the emptiness: the roads abandoned, the villages emptied, until, Deborah sings, "I Deborah arose, that I arose a mother in Israel." A mother in Israel. Not a commander, not a queen, not even a judge, though she was one. She chooses a word from home. Some readers hear in it a whole idea of leadership: care before command, someone who notices who's missing and gets people back on the roads. The song keeps widening the circle. It blesses the leaders who volunteered. It calls to people who ride, people who sit in judgment, people who walk by the way. It imagines the victory retold at the places where people draw water, the ordinary gathering spots, so the good news travels by word of mouth. Then the song turns on itself: "Awake, awake, Deborah: awake, awake, utter a song." Even the singer has to be told to wake up and sing. Rescue isn't finished, the song suggests, until someone remembers it out loud, together, and gives it a tune.

716.title: Sisera's mother at the window (Judges 5:28–30)
716.hook: the song pauses on the enemy's mother, waiting; later tradition hears her cries in the shofar's notes
716.howItsDone: Jews read Sisera's mother in the Song of Deborah, and the Talmud's discussion of the shofar's teruah sound in tractate Rosh Hashanah draws on the verse about her crying, a link remembered when the shofar is blown on Rosh Hashanah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Song of Deborah, which told itself to awake. Your line was a mother in israel. Today, the song finds another mother.

Through a lattice, a woman watches an empty road. The song of victory has been loud: the stars fighting from their courses, the river sweeping the enemy away, Jael blessed in her tent. Then, near the very end, it goes quiet and moves somewhere unexpected. Not to Israel's camp. To the enemy's house. "The mother of Sisera looked out at a window, and cried through the lattice, Why is his chariot so long in coming? why tarry the wheels of his chariots?"
screen: `A WOMAN AT A LATTICE.` → `THE SONG GOES QUIET.` → `WHY IS HIS CHARIOT SO LONG IN COMING?`

segments.voice: You know something she doesn't. Her son is already dead, in a stranger's tent. She's still at the window. Her wisest ladies try to comfort her, and she answers herself with the same words: they must be dividing the spoil. A girl or two for every man. Dyed cloth for Sisera, embroidered on both sides, for the necks of the victors. The song doesn't make her innocent. Her comfort is plunder, and captive women from someone else's town, exactly the kind of victory her son had been winning over Israel. And still the song stays with her: the window, the lattice, the questions, the waiting. Then it ends with a line of its own: "So let all thine enemies perish, O LORD." The song holds both at once: a victory it celebrates, and a mother it can't stop looking at. Jewish tradition kept looking too. Remember teruah, the great shout at Jericho? It's also a shofar call. When the Talmud asks what the teruah of Rosh Hashanah should sound like, it reaches for this verse. The word for her crying, vateyabev, is the clue. The rabbis ask whether her cry was a groan or a sob, and the shofar sounds both. Later tradition hears her cries in the shofar's notes. On the day of judgment, in the middle of the new year's prayers, the sound that wakes the congregation carries the cry of the enemy's mother. Nobody has to excuse what her son did to remember that she waited at a window for someone who wasn't coming home.

717.title: Mighty, while hiding (Judges 6:11–16)
717.hook: the angel calls a frightened man threshing in secret "thou mighty man of valor"
717.howItsDone: Jews study the Gideon chapters as part of the Former Prophets, and rabbinic commentary often asks why a frightened man threshing in hiding was the one chosen.

segments.voice: Yesterday, vateyabev, the cry of Sisera's mother at the window, waiting for a son who wasn't coming home. Your line was the other mother waits. Today, a new judge, found hiding.

A man is threshing wheat in a winepress. Threshing is open-air work: you beat the grain on a flat floor and let the breeze carry the chaff away. Gideon is down in a pit for crushing grapes, out of sight, hiding the wheat from the Midianites, who have raided the harvests until Israel is left with nothing. He's crouched in a hole, beating a little wheat by hand, listening for riders. And under the oak nearby, an angel of the Lord sits watching him. His first words don't fit the scene at all.
screen: `THRESHING IN A WINEPRESS.` → `HIDING THE WHEAT.` → `SOMEONE UNDER THE OAK.`

segments.voice: The angel says: "The LORD is with thee, thou mighty man of valour." Mighty. To a man in a hole. Gideon doesn't say thank you. He asks a hard question: if the Lord is with us, why has all this happened to us? Where are the wonders our fathers told us about, the ones from Egypt? It's a complaint. Some rabbinic readers also hear a man speaking up for his people, and say that's part of why he was chosen. Then the Lord tells him: go in this might of yours, and save Israel. Which might? So far Gideon has hidden wheat and asked why. He says so himself: my family is the poorest in Manasseh, and I am the least in my father's house. The answer isn't a speech about hidden talents. It's this: I will be with you. The strength comes with the promise. And the angel never scolds the fear, or the question. He doesn't wait for Gideon to stop being scared. He calls him mighty while he's still hiding, and lets the name go ahead of him, the way a coat is held out before someone has stood up to put it on.

718.title: Gideon's fleece (Judges 6:36–40)
718.hook: Gideon asks twice for a sign, and receives it
718.howItsDone: Jews read the fleece story in Judges 6 as part of the Former Prophets, and commentators debate whether Gideon's request was a forbidden test of God or a plea for reassurance.

segments.voice: Yesterday, mighty: the angel's name for Gideon while he was still hiding in a winepress. Your line was a coat held out first. Today, the same man, still not sure.

Gideon lays a piece of wool, a fleece, on the threshing floor. Around him, everything is moving. The armies of Midian have crossed over and camped in the valley of Jezreel. Gideon has blown the shofar, and men from several tribes are gathering behind him. He has already been told he'll save Israel. He has already seen fire leap from a rock to take his offering. And still he wants one more sign, and he asks for it to come down with the dew.
screen: `THE ARMIES GATHER.` → `A FLEECE ON THE THRESHING FLOOR.` → `ONE MORE SIGN.`

segments.voice: If there's dew on the fleece only, he says, and the ground around it is dry, then I'll know you will save Israel by my hand, as you said. In the morning he gets up early and wrings out a bowl full of water. The ground is dry. That should be enough. It isn't. So he asks again, and listen to how: "Let not thine anger be hot against me, and I will speak but this once." This time, reverse it: a dry fleece, and dew on all the ground. And that night, the text says, God did so. Dry wool, wet earth. What the story leaves out is any anger. No rebuke, no lecture on faith. The sign is given, and given again, without a word of complaint. That matters, because the Torah also says not to put the Lord to the test. So readers argue over Gideon. Some say he was wrong to ask. Some say he wasn't asking about God at all, but about himself: was he really the one? The story doesn't settle it. It keeps the record: a frightened man doubted, said so out loud, politely, twice, and was answered both times.

719.title: Three hundred (Judges 7)
719.hook: the army is cut to three hundred so no one thinks numbers won
719.howItsDone: Jews read Gideon's three hundred as part of studying Judges, and teachers often point to the stated reason for the cut: so that Israel would not say its own hand had saved it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gideon's fleece, wet and then dry, a doubter's sign given twice. Your line was doubt is allowed. Today, the army he gathered starts to shrink.

Thirty-two thousand men camp by the spring of Harod, with Midian spread out in the valley below. For a man who asked for sign after sign, it should be a comfort. Then the Lord speaks to Gideon, and it's the last thing a nervous general wants to hear. Not: you need more. The opposite. The people that are with thee are too many.
screen: `THIRTY-TWO THOUSAND BY THE SPRING.` → `NOT TOO FEW.` → `TOO MANY.`

segments.voice: The reason is given straight out: "lest Israel vaunt themselves against me, saying, Mine own hand hath saved me." If a big army wins, everyone credits the big army. So the cutting starts. Whoever is fearful and trembling may go home. Twenty-two thousand leave; ten thousand stay. Still too many. Gideon brings them down to the water, and the Lord sorts them by how they drink. Three hundred bring the water up in their hands and lap it. The rest kneel down to drink, and go home. The text never says why lapping was the test; the point seems to be the cut, not the method. Then a tender detail. That night God tells Gideon to attack, and adds: if you're afraid, take your servant Purah and go listen at the edge of the camp first. Even now, the fear is planned for. Gideon overhears a soldier telling a dream: a loaf of barley bread tumbles into the camp and flattens a tent. The battle itself is strange. The three hundred carry shofars, and torches hidden inside empty jars. They surround the camp, smash the jars, blow, and shout: "The sword of the LORD, and of Gideon." Then they stand, each man in his place, and the camp panics and flees. In the story, three hundred were enough, because the numbers were never what won.

720.title: The bramble king (Judges 9:7–15)
720.hook: Jotham's fable: olive, fig and vine refuse to rule; only the bramble wants to
720.howItsDone: Jews study Jotham's fable in Judges 9 as part of the Former Prophets; it is often read alongside Gideon's refusal of kingship in Judges 8 when teachers discuss power and leadership.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the three hundred with jars and torches. Your line was fewer is enough. Today, Gideon is gone, and one of his sons wants to be king.

A voice shouts down from the top of Mount Gerizim to the city of Shechem below. It's Jotham, the youngest son of Gideon, alive because he hid. His half-brother Abimelech has just murdered the rest of the brothers, and the men of Shechem have made Abimelech king. Jotham can't fight him. So he tells them a story about trees. Hearken unto me, he calls down, that God may hearken unto you.
screen: `A VOICE FROM MOUNT GERIZIM.` → `ONE BROTHER ESCAPED.` → `A STORY ABOUT TREES.`

segments.voice: Once, the trees went out to anoint a king. They asked the olive: reign over us. Should I give up my oil, it said, that honors God and people, to go and sway over the trees? They asked the fig. Should I give up my sweetness and my good fruit? They asked the vine. Should I give up my wine, that cheers God and people? Each has real work to do, and won't trade it for a crown. Last, they go to the bramble, a low thorny bush with no fruit worth picking. And the bramble says yes. Come and take shelter in my shade. Some readers smile at that: a bramble has almost no shade to give. Then, in the same breath, a threat: "and if not, let fire come out of the bramble, and devour the cedars of Lebanon." So the fable says two things. The ones with something to give were too busy giving it. The one with nothing to give wanted the crown most, and promised shelter while warning of fire. Jotham turns it on Shechem: if you've dealt honestly with my father's house, enjoy your king. If not, let fire come out of Abimelech and burn you, and fire come out of you and burn him. Then he runs. In the end, Shechem and Abimelech turn on each other and both are destroyed, and the text says the curse of Jotham came upon them.

721.title: Jephthah's vow (Judges 11:29–40)
721.hook: a rash vow ends in tragedy, and the rabbis condemn it
721.howItsDone: Jews study Jephthah's vow with the Talmud and midrash beside the text; the rabbinic tradition treats the vow as rash and wrong, and Jewish law has ways for a vow to be released before a sage or court.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the bramble, the one tree with nothing to give that wanted the crown. Your line was the bramble wants the crown. Today, the end of the week, and a hard story.

Jephthah's brothers drove him out of the house; his mother wasn't their mother. Years later, with the Ammonites at war with Israel, the elders of Gilead come and ask him to lead them. He agrees. The spirit of the Lord comes upon him, the text says. He already has what he needs. Then, on the way to battle, he adds something nobody asked for. A vow. Whatever comes out of the doors of my house to meet me, when I return in peace, shall be the Lord's, and I will offer it up as a burnt offering.
screen: `DRIVEN OUT, THEN CALLED BACK.` → `THE SPIRIT IS ALREADY ON HIM.` → `A VOW NOBODY ASKED FOR.`

segments.voice: He wins, and comes home to Mizpah. Out of the doors comes his daughter, dancing, with timbrels. She was his only child. He tears his clothes. "I have opened my mouth unto the LORD, and I cannot go back." She answers with strange steadiness: do to me what you said. She asks for time to go up into the mountains with her friends and mourn, and he lets her go. When she returns, the text says only that he did with her according to his vow, and that the daughters of Israel went yearly to lament her. She is never named. The rabbis do not admire this. The Talmud names Jephthah among those who asked improperly: what if the thing that came out of the house had been unfit for an offering? A midrash goes further. The vow could have been released; Phinehas the priest was alive then. But Jephthah said, I'm the leader, why should I go to him? And Phinehas said, I'm the high priest, why should I go to him? Between two proud men, a girl was lost. Later commentators even differ on what happened to her: some read the verse as it sounds; some read it as a life set apart. Either way, the rabbis draw the same lesson. A promise made in a rush of feeling, to make sure of something already given, can cost what no one meant to pay.
screen: `OUT OF THE DOORS: HIS ONLY CHILD.` · `I CANNOT GO BACK.` · `THE RABBIS: HE ASKED IMPROPERLY.` · `TWO PROUD MEN, A GIRL LOST.`

segments.voice: Think of the promises that come out of you quickly, sure, no problem, I'll never do that again, and pick one you've made lately. Look for the gap between the feeling and the words, and let it be one breath longer next time. If there's one you can't keep well, notice who you could talk to.
